answer:
Top priorities to strengthen the submission:

1. Fix internal inconsistencies. (a) The plan says registered the company in Milestones, then says no legal entity has been formed. Pick one accurate statement. (b) Payments, damage deposit and verified student onboarding are described as built features in the Solution, yet the $25K ask funds building them. Clarify what exists in the pilot versus what is planned. (c) The 5% capture claim exceeds $50M, but the serviceable market of 6M students at $100-150 is roughly $600-900M, so 5% is about $30-45M. Recompute or correct. (d) The stated fee math is also loose: 15% of $31 is $4.65, but pilot revenue of $291 on $1,940 volume is 15%, so confirm whether the $31 average and $1,940 reconcile with 63 renters (about 31 per renter, not per order).

2. Replace top-down market sizing with bottom-up. $2-3B addressable is built on all 19M students buying formalwear and is not credible as the market for a rental marketplace. Build bottom-up: campuses x active renters x rentals per year x average order x take rate. Use your own pilot conversion (63 of 187 accounts = 34%, one campus) to model per-campus revenue, and show why 600 campuses is the reachable set.

3. Make unit economics and the forecast honest. The 12-month forecast ($9K fee revenue) is tiny relative to a $25K ask and 'break-even on direct costs' is undefined. Show per-campus revenue, ambassador and marketing cost per campus, CAC per renter, contribution margin after payment processing (roughly 3% plus $0.30 on a $36 charge is material against a $4.65 fee), and the damage waiver payout and insurance liability. Explain the claim that CAC stays low with evidence, not assertion. Reconcile 3,500 users and 1,400 renters (40%) with the pilot, and explain how marketing spend of $9K produces that.

4. Quantify the risks that actually kill this model. Address: (a) liquidity and cold start, i.e. how many listings per campus are needed before renters find their size and date, and what pilot data on search-to-rental conversion shows; (b) seasonality, since demand clusters at formal and interview seasons, so annual repeat of 3-4 rentals is unproven and the 44% repeat rate came from a six-week window; (c) trust and safety, including damage, non-return, hygiene and cleaning, disputes, and who is liable; (d) disintermediation, since students can swap Venmo off-platform and the in-person handoff makes leakage easy. State your mitigation and what you will measure.

5. Strengthen evidence quality. The 412-respondent survey and pilot are good, but disclose how the survey sample was drawn (sorority-heavy bias?), whether pilot users were friends of the team, and how many rentals were organic versus founder-driven. Report supply-side metrics: share of 241 listings ever rented, rentals per listing, average lender earnings of $37 over six weeks versus effort, and demand unmet by size or style. Add qualitative quotes and any willingness-to-pay test beyond observed prices.

6. Sharpen competitive and defensibility claims. Name specific competitors (Rent the Runway, Nuuly, Poshmark, campus Facebook groups, university closets and career-center clothing banks) and compare price, speed and trust. 'Density and student org relationships' is a thin moat; add concrete defensibility (exclusive org partnerships, data on sizing and fit, in-app reputation, switching costs) and a plan for expansion to a campus where you have no founder presence.

7. Tighten the ask and milestones. Tie each use of funds to a measurable outcome (e.g., payments live by X date, N listings per campus, Y% repeat rate, Z paid rentals at each of four campuses) and define the specific success criteria for a seed round. Justify $10K for engineering when the CTO is a founder, and explain how ambassador compensation works. Add a timeline with gates.

8. Improve the team section. Add evidence of execution beyond titles (what each person shipped in the pilot), address founder time commitment given all three are students, and note advisor or legal support gaps. Include a plan for graduation timing since two founders are seniors.

9. Presentation. Cut generic claims ('distinctive', 'complementary skills'), lead each section with its strongest number, add a one-line value proposition at the top, and include a simple chart or table for pilot funnel (accounts to listings to requests to completed rentals) and the forecast assumptions so a reader can verify the math in seconds.
